claim: Bacterial type IV secretion systems (T4SSs) can mediate interbacterial DNA transfer through conjugation.
source: Bacterial type IV secretion systems (T4SS) are a diverse class of molecular machines that mediate interbacterial DNA transfer through conjugation as well as delivery of effector proteins into host cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about T4SS function in the introduction.

claim: Bacterial type IV secretion systems (T4SSs) can deliver effector proteins into host cells.
source: Bacterial type IV secretion systems (T4SS) are a diverse class of molecular machines that mediate interbacterial DNA transfer through conjugation as well as delivery of effector proteins into host cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about T4SS function in the introduction.

claim: T4SSs are found in many bacterial species that cause human disease, including Helicobacter pylori, Legionella pneumophila, Bordetella pertussis, Brucella, and Bartonella.
source: T4SSs are found in a wide range of bacterial species, including many species that cause human disease, such as Helicobacter pylori, Legionella pneumophila, Bordetella pertussis, Brucella, and Bartonella (Christie et al., 2014; Grohmann et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Christie et al., 2014 and Grohmann et al., 2018.

claim: T4SSs in Gram-negative bacteria contain a minimum of 12 components designated VirB1-VirB11 and VirD4 in prototype systems.
source: T4SSs in Gram-negative bacteria contain a minimum of 12 components (designated VirB1-VirB11 and VirD4 in prototype systems), organized into an outer membrane core complex (OMCC), an inner membrane complex (IMC), and in some species an extracellular pilus (Christie et al., 2014; Grohmann et al., 2018; Waksman, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Christie et al., 2014; Grohmann et al., 2018; and Waksman, 2019.

claim: T4SSs in Gram-negative bacteria are organized into an outer membrane core complex (OMCC), an inner membrane complex (IMC), and in some species an extracellular pilus.
source: T4SSs in Gram-negative bacteria contain a minimum of 12 components (designated VirB1-VirB11 and VirD4 in prototype systems), organized into an outer membrane core complex (OMCC), an inner membrane complex (IMC), and in some species an extracellular pilus (Christie et al., 2014; Grohmann et al., 2018; Waksman, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Christie et al., 2014; Grohmann et al., 2018; and Waksman, 2019.

claim: High-resolution structures have been determined for OMCCs from Xanthomonas citri T4SS and a portion of the OMCC from the pKM101 conjugation system.
source: High-resolution structures have been determined for OMCCs from two minimized T4SSs (Xanthomonas citri T4SS and a portion of the OMCC from the pKM101 conjugation system) (Sgro et al., 2018; Chandran et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sgro et al., 2018 and Chandran et al., 2009.

claim: T4SSs in Helicobacter pylori and Legionella pneumophila contain additional components not present in minimized systems.
source: T4SSs in several bacterial species, including Helicobacter pylori and Legionella pneumophila, contain additional components, which are not present in the minimized systems (Grohmann et al., 2018; Frick-Cheng et al., 2016; Schroeder, 2017; Ghosal et al., 2017; Chang et al., 2018; Chetrit et al., 2018; Ghosal et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Grohmann et al., 2018; Frick-Cheng et al., 2016; Schroeder, 2017; Ghosal et al., 2017; Chang et al., 2018; Chetrit et al., 2018; Ghosal et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2019.

claim: The H. pylori Cag T4SS translocates CagA, a bacterial oncoprotein, into gastric cells.
source: The Helicobacter pylori Cag T4SS translocates CagA, a bacterial oncoprotein, into gastric cells, contributing to gastric cancer pathogenesis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of the Cag T4SS.

claim: The H. pylori Cag T4SS contributes to gastric cancer pathogenesis.
source: The Helicobacter pylori Cag T4SS translocates CagA, a bacterial oncoprotein, into gastric cells, contributing to gastric cancer pathogenesis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of the Cag T4SS.

claim: The H. pylori Cag T4SS has an OMCC much larger in size and more intricate than those in minimized systems.
source: In addition to containing unique components, the H. pylori Cag T4SS has an OMCC much larger in size and more intricate than those in minimized systems, and contains a periplasmic sub-complex not seen in minimized T4SSs (Grohmann et al., 2018; Chang et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Grohmann et al., 2018; Chang et al., 2018; and Hu et al., 2019.

claim: The H. pylori Cag T4SS contains a periplasmic sub-complex not seen in minimized T4SSs.
source: In addition to containing unique components, the H. pylori Cag T4SS has an OMCC much larger in size and more intricate than those in minimized systems, and contains a periplasmic sub-complex not seen in minimized T4SSs (Grohmann et al., 2018; Chang et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Grohmann et al., 2018; Chang et al., 2018; and Hu et al., 2019.

claim: The structure of the Cag T4SS can be divided into three major regions: the OMCC, a periplasmic ring complex (PRC), and a central stalk.
source: The structure can be divided into three major regions: the OMCC, a periplasmic ring complex (PRC), and a central stalk.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structural analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Cag T4SS OMCC has 14-fold symmetry.
source: We report the structure of a membrane-spanning Cag T4SS assembly, which we describe as three sub-assemblies: a 14-fold symmetric outer membrane core complex (OMCC), 17-fold symmetric periplasmic ring complex (PRC), and central stalk.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structural analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Cag T4SS PRC has 17-fold symmetry.
source: We report the structure of a membrane-spanning Cag T4SS assembly, which we describe as three sub-assemblies: a 14-fold symmetric outer membrane core complex (OMCC), 17-fold symmetric periplasmic ring complex (PRC), and central stalk.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structural analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is an unexpected symmetry mismatch between the OMCC and PRC of the Cag T4SS.
source: Features that differ markedly from those of prototypical T4SSs include an expanded OMCC and unexpected symmetry mismatch between the OMCC and PRC.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structural analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Cag T4SS structure is one of the largest bacterial secretion system assemblies ever reported.
source: This structure is one of the largest bacterial secretion system assemblies ever reported and illustrates the remarkable structural diversity that exists among bacterial T4SSs.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the structural dimensions determined in the study.

claim: The Cag T4SS structure is a large mushroom-shaped complex, approximately 410 Å wide by approximately 460 Å long.
source: The resulting structure is a large mushroom-shaped complex,~410 Å wide by ~460 Å long, with features that closely match those of the Cag T4SS detected in intact H. pylori using cryo-electron tomography (Chang et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2019) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the cryo-EM structure and is shown in Figure 1.

claim: The features of the purified Cag T4SS structure closely match those of the Cag T4SS detected in intact H. pylori using cryo-electron tomography.
source: The resulting structure is a large mushroom-shaped complex,~410 Å wide by ~460 Å long, with features that closely match those of the Cag T4SS detected in intact H. pylori using cryo-electron tomography (Chang et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2019) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citations to Chang et al., 2018 and Hu et al., 2019, and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The global resolution of the Cag T4SS map with no symmetry imposed is 5.4 Å.
source: The global resolution of the map is 5.4 Å when no symmetry is imposed, with the highest resolution regions found near the center of the complex (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A 3.7 Å resolution map of the OMCC was determined using symmetry, focused refinement, and symmetry expansion.
source: Using symmetry, focused refinement, and symmetry expansion, we determined a 3.7 Å resolution map of the OMCC and a 3.5 Å map of the PRC (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a direct result from the cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A 3.5 Å resolution map of the PRC was determined using symmetry, focused refinement, and symmetry expansion.
source: Using symmetry, focused refinement, and symmetry expansion, we determined a 3.7 Å resolution map of the OMCC and a 3.5 Å map of the PRC (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a direct result from the cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The resolution of the OMCC and PRC maps made it possible to trace the secondary structure in these regions.
source: The resolution of the OMCC and PRC maps made it possible to trace the secondary structure in these regions (Figure 1D and Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is stated as a direct result of the high-resolution maps, shown in Figure 1D and Videos 2 and 3.

claim: Only a small number of T4SS particles seen in vitrified ice contained the Stalk density.
source: Since only a small number of T4SS particles seen in vitrified ice contained the Stalk density, it was not possible to determine the symmetry or obtain high resolution of this part of the complex.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM data collection and analysis.

claim: It was not possible to determine the symmetry or obtain high resolution of the Stalk part of the complex.
source: Since only a small number of T4SS particles seen in vitrified ice contained the Stalk density, it was not possible to determine the symmetry or obtain high resolution of this part of the complex.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the structural analysis due to the small number of particles containing the Stalk.

claim: A large cavity runs through the Cag T4SS, starting from where the OMCC spans the outer membrane and extending to the bottom of the PRC.
source: An axial section through the map in Figure 1D shows a large cavity running through the Cag T4SS, starting from where the OMCC spans the outer membrane (OM) and extending to the bottom of the PRC (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structural analysis shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: The tapered end of the Stalk begins in the PRC channel and continues through the inner membrane.
source: The tapered end of the Stalk begins in the PRC channel and continues through the inner membrane (IM).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structural analysis.

claim: Models developed from cryo-ET analyses of both the H. pylori and L. pneumophila T4SSs propose a channel in the Stalk region of the complex.
source: Models developed from cryo-ET analyses of both the H. pylori and L. pneumophila T4SSs propose a channel in this region of the complex (Ghosal et al., 2017; Chang et al., 2018; Chetrit et al., 2018; Ghosal et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ghosal et al., 2017; Chang et al., 2018; Chetrit et al., 2018; Ghosal et al., 2019; and Hu et al., 2019.

claim: A central section through the longitudinal plane of 3D density suggests there may be a channel that runs through the Stalk.
source: A central section through the longitudinal plane of 3D density suggests there may be a channel that runs through the Stalk (Figure 1B,F).
evidence: This is an inference from the structural analysis shown in Figure 1B,F.

claim: Due to the low resolution of the Stalk, the channel through the Stalk cannot be clearly visualized in the 3D map.
source: However, due to the low resolution of the Stalk, this channel cannot be clearly visualized in the 3D map.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the structural analysis.

claim: The OMCC is organized into a central and outer ring connected by 'spokes'.
source: The OMCC, with 14-fold symmetry, makes up the 'mushroom cap' of the T4SS and is organized into a central and outer ring connected by 'spokes' (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structural analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The outer ring of the OMCC surrounds a central chamber that is approximately 270 Å wide and tapers to a approximately 35 Å opening at the top.
source: The outer ring of the OMCC surrounds a central chamber that is ~270 Å wide and tapers to a ~ 35 Å opening at the top (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the structural analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The H. pylori Cag T4SS OMCC contains both an outer layer (O-layer) and a thinner inner layer (I-layer).
source: As seen in OMCCs from minimized T4SSs (Sgro et al., 2018; Chandran et al., 2009), the H. pylori Cag T4SS OMCC contains both an outer layer (O-layer) and a thinner inner layer (I-layer) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structural analysis shown in Figure 3A, and is compared to minimized T4SSs via citations to Sgro et al., 2018 and Chandran et al., 2009.

claim: 'Spokes' and outer rings are visible in both the O-layer and I-layer of the Cag T4SS.
source: 'Spokes' and outer rings are visible in both the O-layer and I-layer of the Cag T4SS (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), but are not present in OMCCs from minimized T4SSs.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structural analysis shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 'Spokes' and outer rings are not present in OMCCs from minimized T4SSs.
source: 'Spokes' and outer rings are visible in both the O-layer and I-layer of the Cag T4SS (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), but are not present in OMCCs from minimized T4SSs.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between the Cag T4SS and minimized T4SSs.

claim: Previous mass spectrometry and Western blot analyses indicated that the isolated Cag T4SS complexes contain CagY, CagX, CagM, CagT, and Cag3.
source: Previous mass spectrometry and Western blot analyses indicated that the isolated complexes contain CagY, CagX, CagM, CagT, and Cag3 (Frick-Cheng et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Frick-Cheng et al., 2016.

claim: Portions of CagY (residues 1677–1816 and 1850–1907), CagX (residues 349–510), and CagT (residues 26–269) can be traced and identified in the cryo-EM map.
source: In the map, we can trace and identify portions of CagY (residues 1677–1816 and 1850–1907), CagX (residues 349–510), and CagT (residues 26–269) (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C, left panels).
evidence: This is a direct result from the structural analysis shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: CagY forms the crest of the cap-like structure of the OMCC and is comprised of β-sheets intertwining to position two helices per protomer atop the cap.
source: CagY forms the crest of the cap-like structure of the OMCC and is comprised of β-sheets intertwining to position two helices per protomer atop the cap (Figure 4A–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, left panel).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structural analysis shown in Figure 4A–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The helices of CagY are predicted to breach the outer membrane, resulting in the formation of a channel.
source: We predict that these helices breach the outer membrane, resulting in the formation of a channel (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the structural analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The C-terminal portion of CagX is comprised of two β-sheets preceded by a long helix.
source: The C-terminal portion of CagX is comprised of two β-sheets preceded by a long helix (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, left panel).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structural analysis shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The long helix of CagX extends from the top of the O-layer through the central chamber into the I-layer of the OMCC.
source: This helix extends from the top of the O-layer through the central chamber into the I-layer of the OMCC (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structural analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A continuous chain 243 residues long corresponding to CagT was traced adjacent to CagX.
source: Adjacent to CagX, we traced a continuous chain 243 residues long corresponding to CagT (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a direct result from the structural analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CagT includes a globular subdomain consisting of two β-sheets followed by a long C-terminal extension of three helices that contribute to the spoke and extend toward the edge of the map.
source: It includes a globular subdomain consisting of two β-sheets followed by a long C-terminal extension of three helices that contribute to the spoke and extend toward the edge of the map (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, left panel).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structural analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A predicted lipidation site within the N-terminal tail of CagT was not observed in the cryo-EM map.
source: A predicted lipidation site within the N-terminal tail of CagT (Fischer, 2011; Akopyants et al., 1998) was not observed in the cryo-EM map, but the N-terminus of CagT is positioned for this interaction with the outer membrane.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the structural analysis, with the prediction supported by citations to Fischer, 2011 and Akopyants et al., 1998.

claim: The N-terminus of CagT is positioned for interaction with the outer membrane.
source: A predicted lipidation site within the N-terminal tail of CagT (Fischer, 2011; Akopyants et al., 1998) was not observed in the cryo-EM map, but the N-terminus of CagT is positioned for this interaction with the outer membrane.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural analysis.

claim: Poly-alanine models of unidentified protein(s) were constructed extending to the edge of the O-layer.
source: Extending to the edge of the O-layer, we have constructed poly-alanine models of protein(s) that we could not identify (Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a direct result from the structural analysis shown in Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The unidentified components in the O-layer fill the remaining density within the spokes and consist predominantly of a repetitive fold composed of repeating units of β-sheets flanked by helices.
source: These components fill the remaining density within the spokes and consist predominantly of a repetitive fold composed of repeating units of β-sheets flanked by helices (Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structural analysis shown in Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Cag3 is predicted to be a component of the OMCC periphery based on a previous study showing that Cag T4SS complexes isolated from a Δcag3 mutant strain lacked peripheral components of the OMCC.
source: We predict that Cag3 is a component of the OMCC periphery based on a previous study showing that Cag T4SS complexes isolated from a Δcag3 mutant strain lacked peripheral components of the OMCC (Frick-Cheng et al., 2016; Hu et al., 2019), but we were unable to obtain a register.
evidence: This prediction is supported by citations to Frick-Cheng et al., 2016 and Hu et al., 2019.

claim: At least two distinct bundles of helices of approximately 200 residues and approximately 300 residues were observed within the I-layer.
source: Within the I-layer we have observed at least two distinct bundles of helices of ~200 residues and ~300 residues (Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structural analysis shown in Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Based on structural studies of the X. citri T4SS, the I-layer of the Cag T4SS is predicted to contain portions of CagY and CagX.
source: Based on structural studies of the X. citri T4SS (Grohmann et al., 2018), the I-layer of the Cag T4SS is predicted to contain portions of CagY and CagX, but none of the poly-alanine models allowed us to unambiguously attribute any portion of CagY, CagX, or other T4SS components to this region.
evidence: This prediction is based on a citation to Grohmann et al., 2018.

claim: The PRC is a short hollow tube, 90 Å tall and 185 Å wide with 96 Å internal diameter.
source: The PRC, with 17-fold symmetry (Figure 4D,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2), is a short hollow tube, 90 Å tall and 185 Å wide with 96 Å internal diameter (Figure 4D,E), connecting the OMCC and the Stalk regions of the Cag T4SS (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the structural analysis shown in Figure 4D,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The PRC connects the OMCC and the Stalk regions of the Cag T4SS.
source: The PRC, with 17-fold symmetry (Figure 4D,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2), is a short hollow tube, 90 Å tall and 185 Å wide with 96 Å internal diameter (Figure 4D,E), connecting the OMCC and the Stalk regions of the Cag T4SS (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structural analysis shown in Figure 1A and Figure 4D,E.

claim: PRCs have not been detected in structural studies of E. coli or X. citri T4SSs.
source: Although PRCs have not been detected in structural studies of E. coli or X. citri T4SSs (Waksman, 2019), this region was identified in cryo-ET studies of both H. pylori and L. pneumophila T4SSs (Ghosal et al., 2017; Chang et al., 2018; Chetrit et al., 2018; Ghosal et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Waksman, 2019.

claim: The PRC region was identified in cryo-ET studies of both H. pylori and L. pneumophila T4SSs.
source: Although PRCs have not been detected in structural studies of E. coli or X. citri T4SSs (Waksman, 2019), this region was identified in cryo-ET studies of both H. pylori and L. pneumophila T4SSs (Ghosal et al., 2017; Chang et al., 2018; Chetrit et al., 2018; Ghosal et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ghosal et al., 2017; Chang et al., 2018; Chetrit et al., 2018; Ghosal et al., 2019; and Hu et al., 2019.

claim: The protein(s) in the PRC region of the cryo-EM maps were modeled as three distinct polyalanine chains.
source: The protein(s) in this region of the cryo-EM maps were modeled as three distinct polyalanine chains (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: This is a direct result from the structural analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–H.

claim: The PRC portion of the H. pylori Cag T4SS structure is predicted to contain CagM.
source: This portion of the H. pylori Cag T4SS structure is predicted to contain CagM (Waksman, 2019; Chang et al., 2018), but the three polyalanine chains could not be unambiguously attributed to CagM or other T4SS components.
evidence: This prediction is supported by citations to Waksman, 2019 and Chang et al., 2018.

claim: The three polyalanine chains in the PRC could not be unambiguously attributed to CagM or other T4SS components.
source: This portion of the H. pylori Cag T4SS structure is predicted to contain CagM (Waksman, 2019; Chang et al., 2018), but the three polyalanine chains could not be unambiguously attributed to CagM or other T4SS components.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the structural analysis.

claim: A symmetry mismatch occurs between the OMCC and PRC, going from 14-fold symmetry in the OMCC to 17-fold symmetry in the PRC.
source: A symmetry mismatch occurs between the OMCC and PRC, going from 14-fold symmetry in the OMCC to 17-fold symmetry in the PRC.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structural analysis.

claim: In the lower resolution structure with no applied symmetry, the OMCC, PRC, and Stalk make physical contact.
source: While the OMCC, PRC, and Stalk make physical contact in the lower resolution structure with no applied symmetry (Figure 5), in the refined structures these connections are lost because of the symmetry mismatch.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structural analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the refined structures, the connections between OMCC, PRC, and Stalk are lost because of the symmetry mismatch.
source: While the OMCC, PRC, and Stalk make physical contact in the lower resolution structure with no applied symmetry (Figure 5), in the refined structures these connections are lost because of the symmetry mismatch.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the symmetry mismatch observed in the structural analysis.

claim: Analysis of the 5.4 Å structure suggests that the connection between OMCC and PRC may occur by contacts between the 14 α-helices extending from the N-terminus of CagX and the 17 unidentified α-helices extending up from the PRC.
source: Analysis of the 5.4 Å structure suggests that the connection between OMCC and PRC may occur by contacts between the 14 α-helices extending from the N-terminus of CagX and the 17 unidentified α-helices extending up from the PRC (Figure 1A,E, and Figure 5).
evidence: This is an inference from the structural analysis shown in Figure 1A,E, and Figure 5.

claim: The tips of the α-helices connecting OMCC and PRC are presumed to be flexible, since the corresponding densities are not well defined in the higher resolution maps.
source: The tips of these α-helices are presumed to be flexible, since the corresponding densities are not well defined in the higher resolution maps (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an inference from the structural analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The H. pylori OMCC is much larger (410 Å diameter) than other structurally characterized OMCCs (225 Å in X. citri and 170 Å in pKM101 conjugation system).
source: Overall, the H. pylori OMCC is much larger (410 Å diameter) than other structurally characterized OMCCs (225 Å in X. citri and 170 Å in pKM101 conjugation system) (Sgro et al., 2018; Chandran et al., 2009) (Figure 6), and the components are more intertwined.
evidence: This is a comparison based on the structural analysis shown in Figure 6, with citations to Sgro et al., 2018 and Chandran et al., 2009.

claim: The components of the H. pylori OMCC are more intertwined than other structurally characterized OMCCs.
source: Overall, the H. pylori OMCC is much larger (410 Å diameter) than other structurally characterized OMCCs (225 Å in X. citri and 170 Å in pKM101 conjugation system) (Sgro et al., 2018; Chandran et al., 2009) (Figure 6), and the components are more intertwined.
evidence: This is a comparison based on the structural analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The dimension of the H. pylori outer membrane pore is 35 Å, which is smaller than the X. citri outer membrane pore (45 Å) but larger than the E. coli outer membrane pore (25 Å).
source: While the inner chamber of the H. pylori OMCC is larger than what is seen in the E. coli and X. citri structures, the dimension of the H. pylori outer membrane pore, at 35 Å, is smaller than the X. citri outer membrane pore (45 Å) but larger than the E. coli outer membrane pore (25 Å) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a comparison based on the structural analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The inner chamber of the H. pylori OMCC is larger than what is seen in the E. coli and X. citri structures.
source: While the inner chamber of the H. pylori OMCC is larger than what is seen in the E. coli and X. citri structures, the dimension of the H. pylori outer membrane pore, at 35 Å, is smaller than the X. citri outer membrane pore (45 Å) but larger than the E. coli outer membrane pore (25 Å) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a comparison based on the structural analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The dimensions of the H. pylori OMCC resemble those of the L. pneumophila Dot/Icm T4SS.
source: The dimensions of the H. pylori OMCC resemble those of the L. pneumophila Dot/Icm T4SS (Ghosal et al., 2017; Chetrit et al., 2018; Ghosal et al., 2019), but there is very little sequence relatedness when comparing components of the H. pylori and L. pneumophila T4SSs, and the L. pneumophila T4SS OMCC has 13-fold symmetry instead of 14-fold symmetry (Chetrit et al., 2018; Ghosal et al., 2019).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citations to Ghosal et al., 2017; Chetrit et al., 2018; and Ghosal et al., 2019.

claim: There is very little sequence relatedness when comparing components of the H. pylori and L. pneumophila T4SSs.
source: The dimensions of the H. pylori OMCC resemble those of the L. pneumophila Dot/Icm T4SS (Ghosal et al., 2017; Chetrit et al., 2018; Ghosal et al., 2019), but there is very little sequence relatedness when comparing components of the H. pylori and L. pneumophila T4SSs, and the L. pneumophila T4SS OMCC has 13-fold symmetry instead of 14-fold symmetry (Chetrit et al., 2018; Ghosal et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between the two T4SSs.

claim: The L. pneumophila T4SS OMCC has 13-fold symmetry instead of 14-fold symmetry.
source: The dimensions of the H. pylori OMCC resemble those of the L. pneumophila Dot/Icm T4SS (Ghosal et al., 2017; Chetrit et al., 2018; Ghosal et al., 2019), but there is very little sequence relatedness when comparing components of the H. pylori and L. pneumophila T4SSs, and the L. pneumophila T4SS OMCC has 13-fold symmetry instead of 14-fold symmetry (Chetrit et al., 2018; Ghosal et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chetrit et al., 2018 and Ghosal et al., 2019.

claim: The C-terminal portion of CagY is structurally similar to VirB10 and TraF homologs.
source: The C-terminal portion of CagY is structurally similar to VirB10 and TraF homologs (Figure 6 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), and the C-terminal portion of CagX is structurally similar to VirB9 and TraO homologs (Figure 6 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a comparison based on the structural analysis shown in Figure 6 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The C-terminal portion of CagX is structurally similar to VirB9 and TraO homologs.
source: The C-terminal portion of CagY is structurally similar to VirB10 and TraF homologs (Figure 6 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), and the C-terminal portion of CagX is structurally similar to VirB9 and TraO homologs (Figure 6 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a comparison based on the structural analysis shown in Figure 6 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both CagY and CagX are much larger in size than characterized VirB/Tra homologs.
